standard.title: Life Cycles
standard.description: compare characteristics of living and non-living things and examine the differences between the life cycles of plants and animals
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify and describe features of living things and group them based on observable characteristics (AC9SFU01, F band; AC9S1U01, 1-2 band). They have not yet formally compared living and non-living things using a characteristic framework, or examined the different structural forms life cycles can take (metamorphic vs non-metamorphic).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students compare characteristics of living and non-living things using observable evidence, and examine how plant and animal life cycles differ in structure — distinguishing metamorphic from non-metamorphic cycles and connecting the physical characteristics of organisms to their life stage.

nodes.label: Living, once living and non-living things have distinct characteristics
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can classify objects as living, once living or non-living and explain their reasoning using observable characteristics (growth, reproduction, response to environment, need for nutrients).
nodes.minimum_width: Students classify a collection of objects as living, once living or non-living and explain the reasoning for at least three classifications using observable characteristics.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the characteristics that distinguish living from non-living things, correctly classify ambiguous cases (dead leaves, fire, crystals, seeds) with reasoning, and distinguish between 'once living' and 'never living'.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians understand and classify the relationships between living things, Country and non-living elements — comparing with the living/non-living framework
Examine edge cases that challenge the classification (viruses, crystals that 'grow', fire that 'spreads') and discuss what characteristic evidence is used to decide
Research how scientists classify single-celled organisms and discuss whether the living/non-living distinction applies at the microscopic level
nodes.hinge_reason: The characteristic-based classification framework is the prerequisite for examining life cycles in Nodes 2 and 3. Students who classify by appearance or familiarity rather than characteristics cannot reason about what changes at each life stage, because they lack a principled definition of what being 'living' involves at any stage.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly classify by appearance or familiarity rather than by characteristics — dead wood is 'non-living' because it looks dead, seeds are 'non-living' because they aren't moving. Making the characteristic evidence explicit (what does living mean? → growth, reproduction, response, needs nutrients) is the scaffold that makes classification reliable across ambiguous cases.

success_criteria: Classifies at least five objects as living, once living or non-living with characteristic-based reasoning
Correctly classifies at least one ambiguous case (e.g. seed, dead leaf, fire) with explanation

nodes.label: Life cycles describe stages of growth and change
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the life cycle of a named plant and a named animal, identifying the stages in sequence and explaining what changes occur at each stage.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the life cycle of one plant and one animal, naming the stages in sequence and describing the key change at each stage.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe and represent the life cycle stages of a plant and an animal, explain what happens at each stage (growth, reproduction, development), and identify similarities and differences between the two cycles.
wider: Represent stages of a plant or animal life cycle using drawings, digital photographs, graphic organisers or physical models — choosing a format that best shows the cyclic nature of the sequence
Investigate how First Nations Australians understand and utilise the life cycles of certain species — examining how knowledge of life stage behaviour guides sustainable harvesting
Compare the life cycle of a plant with that of a single-celled organism (e.g. yeast budding) — exploring what 'life cycle' means across very different living things

response_modes.reason: Students commonly have a narrow life cycle model based on one familiar animal (butterfly or frog). Comparing plant and animal cycles, and examining cycles with different structural forms, builds a more general understanding of what a life cycle is and prevents students from treating one example as universal.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations knowledge of life stage-guided harvesting provides a culturally grounded and ecologically specific direction that goes well beyond identifying stages. The single-celled organism direction challenges students' prototype life cycle model in a genuinely enriching way.
success_criteria: Names the stages of one plant and one animal life cycle in sequence
Describes the key change that occurs at each stage for both organisms

nodes.label: Metamorphic and non-metamorphic cycles differ in structure
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between metamorphic life cycles (dramatic change in body form between stages) and non-metamorphic cycles (gradual growth without structural transformation), and give examples of each.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe one metamorphic and one non-metamorphic life cycle, explaining the key structural difference between them.
nodes.typical_width: Students compare metamorphic and non-metamorphic life cycles across multiple examples (butterflies, beetles, frogs as metamorphic; humans, birds, lizards as non-metamorphic), explain why the physical characteristics of an organism differ across life stages in metamorphic cycles, and represent the comparison.
wider: Compare complete metamorphosis (egg → larva → pupa → adult) with incomplete metamorphosis (egg → nymph → adult) — examining why insects have evolved different developmental strategies
Investigate the physical characteristics of a frog or moth at different life stages and explain how each stage's characteristics suit its role in survival
Research how Maria Sibylla Merian's careful observation across life stages was the first to document metamorphosis — connecting systematic data collection to scientific explanation (AC9S3H01)

response_modes.reason: Students commonly know butterfly metamorphosis as the only metamorphic example and are unaware that beetles, flies, and frogs also undergo metamorphosis. Encountering multiple metamorphic examples across insect and amphibian groups — and contrasting with non-metamorphic examples — builds a more accurate and generalisable concept of metamorphic change.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The complete vs incomplete metamorphosis direction provides genuine conceptual enrichment beyond the Y3 band minimum. The Merian connection (AC9S3H01) offers a historically meaningful link between careful observation across life stages and scientific discovery.
success_criteria: Distinguishes metamorphic from non-metamorphic life cycles with at least one example of each
Explains what 'metamorphosis' means in terms of change in body form between life stages
